notes.reason: The note answers a claim Rees-Mogg does not make. He is careful to separate accession from what happens afterwards: 'everyone who inherits the Crown must take various Protestant oaths on becoming sovereign. So, needs to be a Protestant on succession. But thereafter, they can convert to any religion that he wants.' The note replies that the Crown is limited to Protestant heirs who join in communion with the Church of England, which is the accession rule he has just stated himself, so it argues against something he agrees with. On the point he actually makes the note is at best contested. The Bill of Rights 1689 and the Act of Settlement 1701 set out an automatic forfeiture only for Catholicism: a sovereign who is 'reconciled to or shall hold Communion with the See or Church of Rome or shall professe the Popish Religion' is 'excluded and be for ever uncapeable to inherit possesse or enjoy the Crowne', the Crown passes to the next heir as if that person were dead, and the people are 'absolved of their Allegiance'. I read the Act of Settlement on legislation.gov.uk and it contains no equivalent provision for a reigning sovereign who leaves the Church of England for any other faith. That asymmetry is a well known constitutional anomaly and it is precisely the observation he is making. The note's own sources do not close the gap either: the Wikipedia line that all Supreme Governors since 1701 have been members of the Church of England is a description of what has happened, not a rule about what must happen. Finally, this is Rees-Mogg's specialist subject, he is a Catholic former Leader of the House talking about the very statutes that bar Catholics from the throne, and he would certainly reject a note that tells him the Act of Settlement says something he has just quoted at length.
